extracted.intended_audience: marketing researchers and practitioners interested in online virality and word-of-mouth
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate content characteristics that predict social transmission (virality) of online news/marketing content, and measure their effects controlling for editorial placement and author/article traits. Uses New York Times articles and lab experiments to test hypotheses about emotion and arousal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivity (valence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an article is positive or negative (valence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantified via automated sentiment analysis (LIWC): positivity measured as the difference between the percentage of positive and negative words in an article. Results: more positive content is more likely to be shared; positive-word coefficient larger than negative-word coefficient. Include positivity as a primary predictor in regression models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotionality (affect-ladenness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which an article contains emotional content regardless of valence (overall affect intensity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by LIWC as the percentage of words classified as either positive or negative. More affect-laden content is more likely to make the most-e-mailed list. When controlling for emotionality, positivity still shows independent effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific emotion: Awe
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which content evokes awe (a high-arousal positive emotion of admiration/elevation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manually coded by human raters on a 1–5 Likert scale using title, summary, and full text; awe is positively associated with virality. Examples: scientific discoveries or stories of overcoming adversity. Include awe as a specific predictor; one-standard-deviation increase in awe substantially increases odds of being highly shared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific emotion: Anger
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which content evokes anger (a high-arousal negative emotion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manually coded (1–5 Likert) by independent raters; anger is positively associated with virality, consistent with the arousal hypothesis. Report effect sizes relative to homepage placement/time controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific emotion: Anxiety
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which content evokes anxiety (a high-arousal negative emotion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manually coded (1–5 Likert); anxiety is positively associated with virality. Treat anxiety separately from general negativity because arousal differences produce divergent sharing effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific emotion: Sadness
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which content evokes sadness (a low-arousal or deactivating negative emotion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manually coded (1–5 Likert); sadness is negatively associated with virality. Distinguish sadness from other negative emotions because low arousal reduces sharing likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific emotion: Disgust (control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which content evokes disgust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manually coded and included as a control because prior work linked disgust to transmission; in this data it was not significant. Include when relevant but expect null effects in similar New York Times-style article corpora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activation / Physiological arousal (activation level)
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of physiological arousal induced by content (high vs low activation) that drives action of sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual mediator: high-arousal emotions (awe, anger, anxiety, amusement) increase sharing independent of valence; low-arousal emotions (sadness) decrease sharing. In experiments, measure activation level and test causal mediation from emotion → activation → sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which content contains useful, actionable information (helps readers save money, make decisions, change behavior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manually coded (1–5 Likert). Practically useful articles are more likely to be shared (possible altruistic or reciprocity motives). Include as a content control because practical utility independently predicts virality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which content evokes interest (intrinsic engagement/curiosity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manually coded (1–5 Likert). More interesting articles are more likely to be shared; include as content control. Raters were trained and feedback given on test sets to ensure understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which content evokes surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manually coded (1–5 Likert). Surprise positively linked to sharing. Include as a control for entertainment/self-presentation motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Home page location and prominence (time in page regions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an article appeared on the New York Times home page and how long it spent there (aggregated into seven regions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captured via web crawler every 15 minutes; positions aggregated into seven regions (e.g., top feature, near top feature, right column, middle feature bar, bulleted subfeature, more news, bottom list). Controls: amount of time spent in each region; winsorize top 1% for outliers. Prominence/time on homepage strongly predicts being most-e-mailed, so include these variables to separate editorial placement from content effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance in physical newspaper (section and page)
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper section (e.g., Section A) and page (e.g., A1) where the article appeared in print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encoded as dummy variables to control for physical-paper placement effects; different sections/pages may affect visibility and sharing. Use these as additional external-driver controls in regressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release timing (time of day)
rubrics_metrics.description: Time of day when the article first appeared online (coded e.g., 6 A.M.–6 P.M. vs 6 P.M.–6 A.M. EST).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as a control because release timing may affect attention and sharing; use simple time-of-day dummies or more granular bins as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Day fixed effects / day dummies
rubrics_metrics.description: Controls for day-specific unobserved factors and competition among same-day articles (e.g., world events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include day fixed effects in regression to control for daily variation in baseline sharing rates and concurrent events; cluster standard errors by day of release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author fame (Google hits)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proxy for author prominence measured by the number of Google hits for the first author's full name (logged).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include log(number of Google hits) as a control because famous authors may attract more sharing. Cap or log-transform to reduce skew.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author gender / byline missing
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender of the first author (male, female, unknown/missing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classified using a name-to-gender mapping list supplemented by online lookups; include gender dummies because female authors in this sample were more likely to have their articles shared. Also include an indicator for missing bylines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing complexity (SMOG Complexity Index)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readability / grade-level complexity of writing, measured by the SMOG index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SMOG Complexity Index (McLaughlin 1969) or alternate readability measures; control for complexity because easier/different complexity levels may influence sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word count (article length)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of words in the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include article length because longer articles may contain more information and emotion. In analyses scale (e.g., per 10^3 words) or include as continuous control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding method, reliability, and imputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for measuring content features: automated LIWC coding vs manual human coding; interrater reliability and treatment of uncoded items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated LIWC used for positivity and emotionality (LIWC dictionary ~7630 positive/negative words). For specific emotions and controls (awe, anger, anxiety, sadness, surprise, practical utility, interest), independent human coders rated articles on 1–5 Likert scales; three raters per dimension; interrater reliability α > .70. Scores averaged and standardized. For uncoded articles, assign mean (i.e., standardized zero) and include a dummy for uncoded stories in regressions (standard imputation practice). Provide coders title, summary, link to full text, and detailed instructions; train with feedback on test sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent measures of virality (outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: How virality is operationalized: (1) membership on the New York Times' 24-hour most-e-mailed list (binary), (2) highest rank achieved on the list, and (3) hours (longevity) on the list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary outcome is a binary indicator (ever made the most-e-mailed list); logistic regression with day fixed effects used. Robustness checks: ordered logit on rank (with non-listed coded as 26), OLS on hours on list (noting selection issues because only listed articles have hours>0). Interpret relationships accounting for editorial 'advertising' effects and potential selection into the list.
